content: 1. Clinical research should actively involve community stakeholders, including participants, their partners and families, community members, traditional and religious leaders, or advisory boards. Transparency regarding the aims and interests of all parties involved is essential. 2. Clinical research projects must be based on scientifically justified research questions. Study designs and data collection methods should be efficient and robust enough to generate high-quality evidence and contribute to systematic reviews that inform policies and guidelines. 3. Where feasible, trial activities should be integrated into the work of healthcare points of care to simplify trial conduct. 4. Innovative and adaptive study designs, as well as novel digital technologies such as trial-at-home models, electronic health records, and artificial intelligence, should be considered when they reduce complexity and burden for participants while supporting the generation of reliable evidence. 5. The integrity of scientific data, transparency, and confidentiality of personal data must be ensured at all phases of the study, including planning, conduct, implementation, dissemination of results, and reporting, in accordance with relevant guidelines. 6. Efforts should be made to include under-represented populations, such as children, pregnant and lactating women, and older adults, in clinical research. 7. Researchers should review existing data and literature on the proposed research topic to ensure that new research builds on existing knowledge. Evidence synthesis is a critical component of research, both before and after study completion. 8. Organizations that initiate or fund research should prioritize studies that address important questions relevant to the specific setting and healthcare systems of the communities involved. They should also monitor financial resources and ensure effective budget management. 9. Policies and coalitions, including public-private partnerships, should be supported to create an environment conducive to investing in and participating in reliable local clinical research. 10. Functional, efficient, and effective multi-country systems and coalitions for ethical and regulatory oversight of clinical research should be established and maintained. 11. Patient organizations and communities should be educated, empowered, and supported to understand the value of clinical research. 12. Agreements should encourage open collaboration and data sharing through information technology and electronic health records, avoiding fragmentation of research efforts and capacity. 13. Researchers should improve communication with local communities, policymakers, and clinicians about the potential benefits of clinical research. 14. Member States, international organizations, and sponsors should support the development of local research career structures and training schemes in research ethics, methodology, statistical analysis, research practice, and clinical data management. 15. Investments should be made in creating and maintaining local laboratory infrastructure, sample storage resources, and associated staff capacity to support clinical trials. 16. Participation in external quality assurance schemes should be encouraged and supported. 17. Researchers and funders should collaborate to share experiences, methods, and resources. 18. Regulatory authorities, funders, and researchers should work together to establish or maintain clinical research networks. 19. Regulatory authorities should follow WHO’s guidance on good reliance practices in the regulation of medical products, especially in resource-limited settings. 20. Local clinical trials or special requirements should only be mandated if scientifically justified. 21. Greater financial and human resources should be allocated for training and continuous education on key scientific and ethical considerations for good clinical trials. 22. Good clinical trials should adhere to standards based on key scientific and ethical principles, focusing on the well-being of participants and the reliability of results. 23. Risk-based, proportionate approaches should be adopted in clinical trials. 24. Adequate time and resources should be allocated to ensure properly informed consent, with concise and clear information provided in suitable languages and formats. 25. Innovative methods for obtaining informed consent, such as audiovisual models or electronic consent, should be considered where appropriate. 26. Relevant and easily understandable information should be shared with trial participants at all stages, balancing the duty to inform with the risk of information overload. 27. Patients and communities should be engaged to contribute to the design, execution, and interpretation of clinical trials, enabling effective measures to protect participants’ rights. 28. Priority-setting for clinical research should involve local bodies, patients, and the public, taking into account under-represented groups and vulnerable populations. 29. Local authorities should negotiate with sponsors on how benefits will be shared with the local population before approving studies. 30. Ethical review should ensure sufficient resources are available at study sites to avoid negative impacts on routine patient care. 31. Research projects initiated by sponsors in high-income countries (HICs) should be approved by research ethics committees (RECs) in both the host country and the HIC. 32. Efforts should be made to oppose double standards in research and support equitable, long-term research relationships between partners in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) and HICs. 33. Member States should consider establishing national ethics committees to promote consistency and avoid duplication of work in regions with multiple RECs. 34. Joint RECs or common reviews for multicenter research should be considered in regions or countries. 35. Capacity-building for RECs in resource-limited settings should be supported, including training in scientific research, expedited reviews, and risk-based monitoring. 36. REC reviews should be based on complete, up-to-date protocols and supporting information, ensuring studies are scientifically sound, justified, proportionate, and risk-based. 37. RECs should streamline their internal processes, harmonize with other RECs, and reduce unnecessary bureaucracy. 38. Regional or national forums, databases, or registries should facilitate communication and coordination between RECs. 39. Ethics committees should operate independently of institutional or external pressures and conflicts of interest, making unbiased decisions. 40. International initiatives to strengthen ethical review, including those by WHO, should be supported. 41. Efforts should be made to reduce language barriers in capacity-building by providing documents and organizing events in languages other than English. 42. Researchers should educate community representatives about clinical trials, their differences from routine healthcare, and the protections provided for participants. 43. Formal plans for meaningful communication with participants and the local community throughout the trial should be developed. 44. Communities in resource-limited settings should be empowered to negotiate fair benefits from clinical research, supported by an effective, independent local REC. 45. Funders and research institutions should recognize the value of understanding the study population and its importance for assessing the potential impact and benefit of health research. 46. Community engagement can provide access to valuable information. 47. Research addressing the health needs of children and women, including pregnant and lactating women, should be the norm unless valid justification exists for exclusion. 48. Efforts should be made to recruit diverse and inclusive populations in clinical trials. 49. Both industry-sponsored and academic research in resource-limited settings should focus on relevant research questions addressing clear health needs. 50. Adaptive study designs and data collection should be considered where possible and appropriate. 51. Data collection should focus on variables that provide necessary scientific information for the study, minimizing the burden on local infrastructure and populations. 52. Research protocols should be adapted to local clinical practices and cultural or social considerations, such as visit frequency and sampling. 53. Education on research methodology and study designs in resource-limited settings should be supported, along with building the necessary infrastructure. 54. Researchers should minimize the risk of re-identification of individual participants from shared data and clearly communicate data-sharing plans and risks to participants during informed consent. 55. Academic research institutions and hospitals should support the management, analysis, and publication of clinical research data and results, seeking support for writing and translation when necessary. 56. Funders should accommodate the costs of data-related activities when funding clinical research. 57. Funders and sponsors should allocate dedicated human resources for communicating validated information and research results to participants, communities, clinicians, policymakers, the media, and the general public. 58. More research should address the needs of women of childbearing age, including pregnant and lactating women. 59. Ethical guidelines emphasize the inclusion of women in research, including pregnant and lactating women, unless there are valid reasons for exclusion. 60. Physiological differences should not exclude populations from research where results may benefit them, provided risks are understood and safeguards are in place. 61. Researchers and ethics committees should respect cultural contexts when conducting studies involving women of childbearing age, including pregnant and lactating women. 62. Pregnancy registries in LMICs should be established and utilized. 63. Clinical trials in children should be considered from the outset at all stages of clinical development. 64. Studies in children are needed across healthcare settings, including hospitals and communities, even in remote areas.
